items.title: 54270_Doc Cheatham oral history interview
items.q: Damn, Roy at the Three Deuces, what the hell is this, then I'd come and I'd hear Jabbo.

ctx.x: I wanted to play. I wanted to play, that was the only thing. And I was confused. Cause then I'd hear Charlie Shavers, I wanted to throw my horn away. I said

I'd hear what is this? Damn, Roy at the Three Deuces, what the hell is this, then I'd come and I'd hear Jabbo. I'd hear Cuban Cube, man, I didn't know what to do, I said, damn, that was my problem. I wanted to play. Money didn't mean anything to me. That's why I worked for Sam Wooding for $75.00 to Europe. I wasn't worried about money, because I was sitting beside Tommy Ladner, side-talking to Ladner.
Where did you hear Jabbo Smith?

items.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995
items.q: like Roy and Freddie Webster and all these beboppers

ctx.x: Was that a tough time also?

During those days, the Latin musicians from Latin countries like Puerto Rico came in. Bands. Musicians. And they started, they had a dancing school and they had a band in there that played all Latin music. And it got to the place where that’s all the people wanted was Latin music. And the bands would come in and Machito came in to organize a band and Tito Puente came in overnight. Because I taught Marcelino trumpet, but he could never learn. He had one of the greatest Latin bands that there ever was in the world…

he came out all of a sudden. Charles Parker came out and drive everybody crazy, and the followers followed him. That’s what you have now. You have more alto saxophone players now than there ever was. And they all can play, and some good ones, you’ve got some, I think, what’s the guy name that wears that leather cap all the time, I forget. But I think he’s better than Charlie Parker. But you’ve got a lot of them. And you’ve got a lot of Dizzy. That’s the way it started. And you can forget about jazz in those days.…
